title: Report on a Dispatched Clerkship in Hepato-Pancreato-Biliary Surgery at the Chinese University of Hong Kong
paragraphs: I was allowed to study abroad in hepato-pancreato-biliary surgery at the Chinese University of Hong Kong and did a two-month clerkship.

In the autumn when I attended the briefing on the clinical clerkship dispatch program, I keenly felt that I lacked both language ability and medical knowledge. Even so, out of a strong wish not to miss this valuable opportunity, I started studying English from that day. There was an opportunity within the university to take polyclinic clerkships together with exchange students, and as I spoke to them actively and learned about the healthcare systems of their home countries and about life in Japan, I was able to advance my preparation both in language ability and in mindset. After the study abroad was decided, in the pre-departure lectures I received valuable talks from many doctors. Every doctor spoke passionately about their experiences as students, and my expectation and motivation grew even more.

Hong Kong does not have a universal health insurance system like Japan's, and there is no fee schedule system either. Everything is self-pay, and three kinds of medical institutions function: public hospitals, private hospitals and clinics. Public hospitals are inexpensive but have very long waiting times, while private hospitals are expensive but one can be seen immediately. Also, there is no employment relationship between doctors and hospitals, and payments from patients are distributed between the hospital and the doctor. For that reason, the salaries of doctors at public hospitals are relatively low. The Prince of Wales Hospital, where I did my clerkship, is the hospital affiliated with the Chinese University of Hong Kong, suffers from a serious shortage of doctors, and it was impressive to see foreign doctors who cannot speak Cantonese and doctors from mainland China who are weak in English cooperating and devoting themselves to clinical work, education and research.

Charts are in English, and medical students are educated in English, so I had no trouble except in conversations in outpatient practice and during surgery. In the first half, I took part in the local sixth-year surgery rotation. Since the local students take an OSCE exam on ward patients at the end of each departmental clerkship, they studied desperately from examination through to the initial treatment plan. The lectures were also practical and interactive, and in their free time they practised on their own with the patients' cooperation. Within that, I had opportunities to take histories and do physical examinations in English with patients fluent in English, which was a valuable experience of testing in practice what I had prepared beforehand. In the second half, I mainly observed surgery. The doctors and nurses were very friendly and looked after me, who was in the operating room all day every day. Discussing the nanoknife operation for pancreatic cancer, which is not yet performed in Japan, was impressive, and we were able to exchange opinions on the current situation and outlook. I was also very interested in hilar cholangiocarcinoma at the Department of Surgical Oncology of Nagoya University, and shared my experience within the university and the doctors' knowledge. I realised anew how wonderful the environment I belong to is, and strongly thought that I want to work hard so that my generation can contribute further to its development in the future. Hong Kong surgeons differ from Japan in that they themselves also perform endoscopic examination and treatment. In particular, Professor Philip, the president of the Chinese University of Hong Kong, is a pioneer who performed the first ESD (endoscopic submucosal dissection) in Hong Kong in 2004 and is now also involved in the development of surgical robots. Since I myself was interested in robotics, after talking with the professor I was kindly allowed to visit the largest science and technology development centre in Hong Kong, and I received great stimulation.

Hong Kong is a big city where about 7 million people live in an area about half the size of Tokyo, and I was able to get used to life there right away. I stayed in a student dormitory on the hospital grounds, and the ward and operating rooms were a five-minute walk away. I went out to eat with the local students almost every day and built deep friendships. It was very impressive to see them talk with irony about social entanglements, and it was valuable learning through contact with a different culture. The student dormitory was a little old, and the kitchen and shower were shared. As an aside, on the day I arrived I found a gecko with a big belly in my room, two weeks later her young were born, and by the day I left they had grown big. I remember being deeply moved as I overlapped my own daily growth with this small gecko.

Finally, I would like to express my heartfelt thanks to everyone at the International Collaboration Office, beginning with Dr. 粕谷, Dr. 長谷川 and Dr. Itzel, who guided and supported me in the preparation for this study abroad, Professor Chok, who looked after me there, and Dr. 高見秀樹 and Professor 近藤豊, who guide me regularly in Japan.
